explanation: Fires on the pronoun 'it' (also 'It', Danish 'Det') used as a clause subject, most strongly right after a conjunction or discourse connective such as 'And', 'as', 'so', 'if' or 'Then', or at the start of a new sentence. Object 'it', 'its' and other tokens give only weak activation.

Fires on the first function word or punctuation after a short opening phrase at the very start of a document or title, e.g. the preposition after a title noun phrase ('Insecticide interaction[with]', 'HIV-1 variants[in]'), 'do' in 'How do', 'a/an' in 'There's a', or ':' and '--' after a headline name. It responds to position, about the 2nd to 5th token of a document or heading, more than to token identity. Mid-document function words are weak.

Fires on tokens inside boilerplate or structured scholarly and code material: the year digit in 'Copyright (c) 20[1]x', decimal points and numbers in LaTeX or figure markup, '[' after a YAML front-matter '---', 'Fig' references, and pieces of Latin species or drug names in scientific abstracts. Ordinary prose is weak. A mixture of 'technical document formatting' contexts with no single token type.

Fires on tokens inside news-style text about conflict, security, politics and law enforcement (armed groups, invasion, police, intelligence, corruption, protests, sanctions). It often peaks on the verb or function word that links actors to the conflict ('formed to[resist]', 'fighting[the]', 'after[authorities]'). Topic context matters more than the token itself.

Fires on the second member of a paired or contrastive construction, at the point where a comparison or pairing is set up: 'before[and] after', 'heavy[vs]. light', 'the[same]', 'every[second]', 'object[sender], EventArgs', citation ranges '[@B1[-]'. Also fires on assorted unrelated tokens (word pieces, 'AND NOW'). The connecting idea is weak.

Fires on a token that completes a common multi-word phrase or reporting idiom, where the next word is highly predictable: 'little[is] known', 'long[way]', 'at[least]', 'Nice[to] meet', 'work[to] do', 'officials[said]', 'For more[information]', 'is no[more]'. Context-driven phrase completion, not a specific token.

Fires on the second digit of a four-digit year, i.e. the '0' in '20xx' or the '9' in '19xx' (or the space before the year), in dates, legal case dates and copyright lines. It is strongest in formal full dates ('November 15, 1[9]55'). Other digits and numbers that are not years are weak.

Fires mostly in programming or technical Q&A contexts on tokens that start a member, attribute or path element (CSS property 'width', 'super', 'console', 'parent', URL path segments like '/angular') and on 'so' in 'and so on/forth'. The 'and so on' and code-identifier parts look like separate jobs, plus scattered prose tokens.

Fires on a preposition that is required by the preceding word or phrase, mostly in fixed combinations ('indissociable[from]', 'with respect[to]', 'exception[to]', 'prior[to]', 'in front[of]', 'ahead[of]', 'lighter[than]'). Also fires on string-concatenation operators ('&', '+') that join operands. Prepositions not selected by the head are weak.

Fires on mid-word or mid-compound continuation pieces and modifier tokens (e.g. 'irre[vers]ibly', 'intrins[ically]', 'top[-to]-bottom', 'hand[-foot]', 'Kin[vey]') and on year digits in URLs or dates. These share no obvious meaning.

Fires on the line-ending token in indented code or markup (';
', ')
', '>
', '}
', ',
', '"
') that closes a statement or element and is followed by an indented next line. It is strongest in deeply nested code. Prose newlines are weak.

Fires on tokens in medical or clinical text, especially word pieces that complete disease, treatment or drug terms ('contr[actions]', 'malign[ancy]', 'Hem[ophilia]', 'COP[D]', '[onc]ology', 'short[ness]'). There are also scattered unrelated hits in legal and sentencing text and in code.

Fires on assorted tokens: word-piece completions of names and terms ('at[ax]ia', 'Gal[era]', 'pain[less]'), 'me' in idioms like 'let me' and 'believe me', and the second number in sports scores ('7-[3]', '2-[0]'). No common thread is evident.

Fires in source code on the second part of a dotted or compound identifier, such as a qualified name, method or attribute ('javax.annotation[.Non]null', 'Crypto[.Public]Key', 'pygame.time[.Clock]', 'setLocation[RelativeTo]', 'android[:text]'). It is strongest just after a '.' or at a camel-case boundary. A few weak hyphenated-compound hits occur in prose.

Fires on the middle or final word piece of a word split into several tokens, often rare, technical or foreign words ('Water[gate]', 'subd[ural]', 'immunoh[isto]chemistry', 'cor[pos]', 'micro[grams]', 's[ipped]'). The token's role as a non-initial fragment of a known word matters more than meaning.

Fires on the word right after the subject noun phrase of an expository statement, typically the verb or adverb ('absorbers[are] generally', 'are[commonly] known', 'experiments[show]', 'Airport[covers]'). It is strongest in technical or patent-style descriptive prose. Scattered code tokens also fire.

Fires on tokens in non-English text (French, Dutch, Portuguese), especially verbs and negation ('sont', 'niet', 'estar', 'se'), and on interior pieces of uncommon proper names in English text ('Rem[ig]ius', '[Ach]onee', 'N[ighth]awks'). Two loosely related jobs, both about unfamiliar or foreign word forms.

Fires on a mixture: commas and parentheses in formal, patent or scientific prose ('including[,]', 'such as[,]', 'fetuses[ (]'), 'to' after verbs like 'aimed' or 'stands', and assorted code, CJK and number tokens. No single clear role.

Fires on the word right after an existential or modal frame, the quantifier or verb that states what exists or is possible: 'There is[nothing]', 'There is[every] reason', 'There[are]', 'do[everything] we can', 'all that we[can]', 'should[be] able', 'We have[no] doubt'. Ordinary predicates are weak.

Fires on the article or determiner that opens a predicate or partitive phrase after a short copular or partitive frame: 'X is[a]', 'It's[an]', 'One of[the]', 'Many of[the]', 'such[a]'. It is strongest in short definitional sentences at the start of a text. Articles in other positions are weak.

Fires on the word piece after a 'pro' prefix or a 'pro'-initial token in a split word: 'proph' (prophylaxis, prophetic), 'prost' (prostaglandin, prostheses), 'prof', 'prox' and 'Pro[ff]itt'. Activation is driven by these 'pro-' word fragments; other words are weak.
